name: Celtuce
summary: A lettuce crop type selected for its enlarged edible stem. It is horticulturally distinct from head and leaf lettuce, but remains within Lactuca sativa; this is not a named cultivar.

identity.guidance: UC Davis and NC State use Celtuce for stem lettuce within Lactuca sativa. POWO recognizes the species; the crop-group name does not establish a separate species or cultivar.

growth.short: Annual lettuce with an enlarged tender stem
growth.guidance: The edible stalk is the distinguishing harvested structure. Cultivar and harvest stage affect stalk size; no fixed mature dimensions are assigned to the crop group.

cultivation.short: Grow as a lettuce crop; harvest before the stalk becomes coarse
cultivation.guidance: Extension descriptions identify the swollen stem as the crop objective. Detailed spacing, indoor lighting, hydroponic compatibility and a universal harvest date are not established for this identity.

propagation.short: Seed-grown lettuce crop; cultivar-specific protocol not assigned
propagation.guidance: Celtuce is grown from lettuce seed. The selected references do not provide a distinct seed-starting protocol separate from general lettuce practice; use the seed supplier's instructions for a named strain.

harvestUse.short: Harvest the tender stem; leaves may also be used
harvestUse.guidance: Celtuce is valued chiefly for its thick stem, used as a vegetable. The sources describe the crop distinction but do not establish one cultivar-independent harvest size.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No cited source evaluates this crop type in a hydroponic system.

evidence.note: Lettuce crop type selected for an enlarged stem.

height.reason: No comparable mature dimension is established for the crop group.

spread.reason: No comparable mature dimension is established for the crop group.

spacing.reason: No spacing recommendation is assigned from the selected crop-group sources.

light.reason: Outdoor crop guidance is not translated into indoor grow-light intensity.

name: Flax
summary: An annual crop grown for fiber or seed. The intended use and cultivar affect harvest and processing; this species-level profile does not promise a dual-purpose result.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Linum usitatissimum. Flax and linseed refer to use of the same crop species; fiber and oilseed types are not interchangeable cultivar claims.

growth.short: Annual, upright crop; fiber and seed forms differ
growth.guidance: USDA crop guidance treats flax as an annual field crop and distinguishes production purposes. No garden-scale mature size or container suitability is inferred.

cultivation.short: Use a locally adapted seed lot and the intended fiber/oilseed production guide
cultivation.guidance: The cited USDA crop guidance is for agricultural production, not indoor or hydroponic systems. Soil, seeding rate and harvest recommendations must be selected for the actual cultivar and purpose.

propagation.short: Seed-grown crop; no home seed-start protocol assigned
propagation.guidance: Flax is propagated by seed, but the selected crop reference is not a home-garden germination protocol. Exact sowing depth, temperature and seedling handling remain needs-validation for a household setting.

harvestUse.short: Harvest use depends on fiber versus mature seed production
harvestUse.guidance: Flax is cultivated for stem fiber or seed/linseed. This profile does not prescribe a harvest stage without a documented cultivar and intended use.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No cited source establishes hydroponic production suitability.

evidence.note: Annual crop form; cultivar and use type unspecified.

spacing.reason: Field seeding rates are not converted into garden or pod spacing.

light.reason: Crop cultivation evidence does not define an indoor light category.

name: Rice
summary: A globally important cereal with major cultivar and production-system variation. This species profile does not imply that grocery rice is viable seed or suitable for a home pond/container.

identity.short: Accepted cultivated rice species Oryza sativa
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Oryza sativa. Cultivars and subspecies differ; no japonica/indica assignment is made without seed-lot evidence.

growth.short: Annual cereal grass; cultivar and water regime matter
growth.guidance: USDA crop documentation describes rice as an annual grain crop with production systems that include flooded and non-flooded conditions. It does not establish household-container dimensions or yield.

cultivation.short: Do not infer a universal flooded-water requirement
cultivation.guidance: Rice production systems are not identical; the cited USDA source discusses crop production, not a home hydroponic recipe. Water depth, irrigation, climate fit and cultivar selection remain system- and region-specific.

propagation.short: Seed-grown crop; seed lot and sowing system must be verified
propagation.guidance: Rice is propagated by grain seed in crop production. The selected reference does not establish grocery-grain viability or a reliable household germination protocol, so those details remain unresolved.

harvestUse.guidance: The edible product is the mature grain. Harvest timing, drying and milling depend on cultivar and production system and are not generalized here.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Flooded-field production evidence is not proof of compatibility with recirculating hydroponics.

height.reason: No cultivar-specific home-growing dimension is provided.

spread.reason: No household spacing or spread is provided.

spacing.reason: Agricultural seeding rates are not mapped to home or pod spacing.

name: Spring Barley
summary: A spring-sown barley crop type, not a cultivar. Field production guidance is useful for crop context but does not establish a small-container or indoor grain protocol.

identity.short: Accepted species Hordeum vulgare; spring crop type
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Hordeum vulgare. Spring barley describes a production/lifecycle type within the species, not a separate species or named cultivar.

growth.guidance: University of Minnesota Extension describes spring barley development as a field crop. Its stage and height vary with cultivar and growing conditions; no household mature size is assigned.

cultivation.short: Establishment depends on cool-season timing and seedbed conditions
cultivation.guidance: UMN reports barley germination can begin at low soil temperatures and warns against planting deeper than the coleoptile can emerge. Its field guidance is not converted to container spacing or an indoor light prescription.

propagation.short: Seed-grown cereal; field germination data only
propagation.guidance: Barley is established from grain seed. UMN's minimum temperature and planting-depth guidance is field-crop evidence; it does not specify a household seedling protocol or indoor germination-light requirement.

harvestUse.short: Grain or forage use depends on the selected type
harvestUse.guidance: Spring barley is grown for grain or forage in agricultural systems. This record does not assume malting quality or a specific end use for an unnamed seed lot.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Field cereal guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: Spring-sown barley crop type; cultivar unspecified.

name: Grain Sorghum
summary: A warm-season grain crop within Sorghum bicolor. It is kept distinct from forage sorghum-sudangrass hybrids; field-scale drought traits do not establish container suitability.

identity.short: Sorghum bicolor; grain-crop type, no cultivar assigned
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Sorghum bicolor. The profile is restricted to grain sorghum and does not inherit forage-hybrid management or cultivar-specific grain traits.

growth.short: Warm-season annual grass grown for grain
growth.guidance: USDA crop information describes sorghum as a warm-season grain crop. Plant height and maturity differ by cultivar and use; no single dimension is assigned.

cultivation.short: Warm-season establishment; use grain-sorghum guidance, not Sudex forage rules
cultivation.guidance: Extension crop references distinguish grain sorghum from sorghum-sudangrass forage. The available drought-tolerance evidence is not a watering prescription and does not establish indoor or hydroponic use.

propagation.short: Seed-grown crop; exact household sowing conditions unresolved
propagation.guidance: Grain sorghum is seeded as a crop. Field rates and planting depths are not converted to home-container instructions; use the seed supplier's cultivar-specific directions.

harvestUse.short: Mature grain; end use depends on grain type
harvestUse.guidance: The profile represents sorghum grown for grain, not forage biomass. Food/feed handling and maturity are not generalized without the seed lot's intended use.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Field production sources do not evaluate this crop in hydroponics.

evidence.note: Warm-season grain crop; forage hybrids excluded.

spacing.reason: Field seeding rates do not define pod or container spacing.

name: Proso Millet
summary: A short-season annual cereal grain. It is distinct from pearl, foxtail and Japanese millets; cultivar and end use are not specified.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Panicum miliaceum as proso/common millet. Other crops called millet belong to different species and are not included in this identity.

growth.guidance: USDA crop guidance treats proso millet as a grain crop. Regional varieties and production systems determine maturity and stature; household dimensions are not established here.

cultivation.short: Select an adapted grain variety; avoid transferring forage-millet rates
cultivation.guidance: Crop production sources treat proso separately from forage millets. The cited data are not a home-container prescription and do not establish hydroponic suitability.

propagation.short: Seed-grown grain; home sowing details need cultivar-specific evidence
propagation.guidance: Proso millet is grown from seed. Field-crop seeding rates are not converted into pot spacing or an indoor germination protocol.

harvestUse.guidance: This identity represents proso millet grain, but the source does not establish processing or culinary instructions for an unidentified seed lot.

name: Adzuki Bean
summary: A warm-season pulse grown for dry mature seeds. It is a distinct Vigna species, not mung bean or common bean; field-crop evidence should not be read as a compact garden recommendation.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Vigna angularis. Adzuki/azuki is distinct from Vigna radiata (mung bean) and Phaseolus vulgaris (common bean). No cultivar or seed color is assigned.

growth.short: Warm-season annual legume; growth habit varies by type
growth.guidance: University of Wisconsin crop guidance describes adzuki as a field pulse. The species-level record does not identify a bush or climbing cultivar or assign a mature height.

cultivation.short: Warm soil and a frost-free growing window are important
cultivation.guidance: UW crop guidance reports slow emergence in cool soil and better establishment in warm conditions. Its commercial dates, rates and row widths are not transplanted as garden spacing.

propagation.short: Seed-grown pulse; field emergence guidance only
propagation.guidance: Adzuki is established from seed. The cited field source reports emergence timing that varies with soil warmth; it does not document a home tray protocol or a cultivar-specific germination temperature.

harvestUse.short: Dry mature beans; harvest and food preparation depend on intended use
harvestUse.guidance: The cited crop reference describes adzuki as a pulse crop. No fresh-pod harvest stage or cooking/safety instruction is added without a directly supporting source.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Field pulse guidance does not establish hydroponic production suitability.

growthHabits.reason: The identity has no specified bush/vining cultivar and the source does not resolve this record's habit.

spacing.reason: Field crop row spacing is not a home-garden or pod-spacing recommendation.

light.reason: No indoor grow-light requirement is established.

name: Pigeon Pea
summary: A warm-climate perennial legume commonly grown as an annual food crop outside the tropics. This species profile does not imply a dwarf cultivar or container suitability.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Cajanus cajan. Common names include pigeon pea, gandul and guandú; no regional landrace or cultivar is specified.

growth.short: Woody perennial legume; often managed as an annual crop
growth.guidance: USDA NRCS describes a long-lived, warm-season legume that may become shrub-like. The crop guide is not evidence of compact growth or indoor suitability.

cultivation.short: Warm conditions and establishment after frost risk
cultivation.guidance: USDA NRCS guidance describes warm-soil establishment and regional use. It is a field/forage and food-crop source; no exact Garden X system compatibility, spacing or hydroponic claim is made.

propagation.short: Seed-grown legume; alternate transplanting protocol is crop-specific
propagation.guidance: Pigeon pea is commonly raised from seed; an ICRISAT nursery/transplant protocol exists for agricultural systems. This does not establish a household seed tray schedule or cultivar-specific germination values.

harvestUse.short: Pods may be harvested green or seeds mature and dry
harvestUse.guidance: Pigeon pea is used as a food legume, but the referenced USDA plant guide does not define cultivar-specific harvest timing. Select use and maturity from the seed supplier or regional crop guidance.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Agricultural soil and forage guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: Species can develop a woody shrub habit; stature depends on cultivar and climate.

height.reason: No cultivar or regional mature height is specified.

spread.reason: No cultivar or regional mature spread is specified.

spacing.reason: Field plant spacing is not container or pod spacing.

name: French Sorrel
summary: A perennial sorrel grown for its tart leaves. The common name sorrel spans several genera and species; this profile is restricted to Rumex scutatus.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Rumex scutatus. It is not Oxalis and should not be confused with field sorrel or other Rumex species sold under broad common names.

growth.short: Low perennial herb with edible leaves
growth.guidance: NC State describes French sorrel as a low, creeping perennial, usually 2 ft tall and forming a clump up to 3 ft wide in its regional account. These are regional species ranges, not container guarantees.

cultivation.short: Perennial leafy herb; protect quality by harvesting young leaves
cultivation.guidance: NC State lists full sun to partial shade and average, medium, well-drained soil. It notes removing flowers promptly to promote leaf growth. This is outdoor regional guidance, not an indoor-light or hydroponic recommendation.

propagation.short: Seed is listed; germination protocol remains unestablished
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed as a propagation strategy but the selected page does not specify sowing depth, germination temperature, duration, or seedling care. Those seed-stage details remain needs-validation.

harvestUse.short: Leaves used as a tart culinary green
harvestUse.guidance: French sorrel leaves are edible and tart. This profile does not provide safety or dietary advice beyond the cited horticultural identification.

problems.short: No known insect pests or diseases reported by NC State
problems.guidance: The NC State species page reports no known diseases or insect pests in its regional profile. This is not a guarantee of pest-free growth in every location.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected source does not assess hydroponic production.

spacing.reason: No documented garden spacing is assigned.

light.reason: Outdoor exposure is not represented as indoor light intensity.

name: Cardoon
summary: A large thistle-like edible crop grown chiefly for blanched leaf stalks. It shares a species with globe artichoke horticultural forms; this record is cardoon and does not assert an artichoke cultivar.

identity.short: Cynara cardunculus; cardoon type, no named cultivar
identity.guidance: POWO accepts Cynara cardunculus. NC State describes cardoon and globe artichoke within the species complex; the edible harvested part and horticultural group distinguish this record from globe-artichoke profiles.

growth.short: Large, upright herbaceous perennial, sometimes grown as an annual
growth.guidance: NC State reports a broad regional size range of roughly 3–6 feet tall and 2–3 feet wide and describes deeply cut prickly foliage. These are outdoor regional dimensions, not container sizing.

cultivation.short: Full sun, moist well-drained soil; allow substantial space
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun and rich, moist but well-drained soil. The page also flags prickles, wind damage and potential naturalization; suitability depends on local climate and invasive status.

propagation.short: Seed and vegetative routes are documented
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed, division and root cuttings. The cited page does not provide germination parameters; use seed-supplier instructions for sowing details, or a documented vegetative route when appropriate.

harvestUse.short: Blanch and cook the young leaf stalks
harvestUse.guidance: NC State identifies emerging leaf stalks as the principal vegetable harvest and says they are blanched, harvested and cooked. Do not substitute the edible flower-bud use of globe artichoke.

problems.short: Spines, wind damage and regional spread are relevant
problems.guidance: NC State reports prickly stems, possible wind damage, root rot, gray mold, powdery mildew, slugs and aphids; it warns cardoon can spread in some regions. Local invasive status matters.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No hydroponic trial or system guidance is cited.

spacing.reason: The cited source's available-space category is not converted to exact spacing.

light.reason: Full-sun outdoor evidence is not mapped to indoor grow-light requirement.

name: Horseradish
summary: A hardy perennial grown primarily for its pungent root. Root pieces readily produce new plants, so choose a contained location; seed is not the usual represented propagation material.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Armoracia rusticana. Horseradish is distinct from radish (Raphanus sativus); the edible root is the principal horticultural product.

growth.short: Perennial herb with deep, spreading roots
growth.guidance: NC State describes a perennial plant reaching approximately 2–5 feet tall and 2–4 feet wide in its regional profile. Root fragments can resprout, which affects containment.

cultivation.short: Plan for root spread and harvest access
cultivation.guidance: The NC State source describes root cutting/division propagation and notes the plant can spread from root pieces. Use a contained bed or container only with adequate root volume; no exact pot size is established.

propagation.short: Root cuttings or division are the practical documented routes
propagation.guidance: NC State lists root cuttings and division. These vegetative methods establish the plant from root material; seed germination and seedling establishment are not documented in the selected source.

harvestUse.short: Harvest and process the pungent root
harvestUse.guidance: Horseradish is grown for its edible root, which is grated/prepared for culinary use. The cited source does not give a universal harvest age or processing protocol.

problems.short: Root fragments may persist and spread
problems.guidance: NC State warns that horseradish can spread from roots. Remove unwanted fragments and check local guidance before planting near natural areas.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No source evaluates horseradish in hydroponics.

evidence.note: Perennial plant that can spread through root material.

spacing.reason: Dimensions are not converted into exact planting spacing.

light.reason: No indoor grow-light classification is established.

name: Prickly Pear Cactus
summary: A domesticated edible cactus grown for both young pads (nopales) and fruit (tuna). This species is distinguished from the many other Opuntia species also called prickly pear.

identity.guidance: POWO accepts Opuntia ficus-indica. Common names nopal, tuna and Indian fig cactus are used; generic prickly pear can refer to many Opuntia species, so this entry is taxonomically restricted.

growth.guidance: Kew describes a succulent shrub or tree; University of Arizona's campus arboretum describes the domesticated food plant and pad propagation. Mature form varies with cultivar and climate; no single dimensions are assigned.

cultivation.short: Warm, arid-adapted crop; use a well-drained site
cultivation.guidance: University of Arizona documents the edible cactus in arid-region cultivation and pad establishment. Its regional guidance should not be generalized to wet climates or used to infer indoor/hydroponic performance.

propagation.short: Rooted pads are the documented practical route
propagation.guidance: University of Arizona describes callusing a pad cutting before planting it shallowly in dry soil. This is vegetative propagation and preserves the selected plant; no seed-germination protocol is claimed.

harvestUse.short: Young pads and fruit are edible after careful spine/glocid removal
harvestUse.guidance: University of Nevada Extension describes pads and fruit as edible and emphasizes careful harvest and preparation. Remove glochids and spines safely; the source is food-handling guidance, not medical advice.

problems.short: Spines and glochids are a handling hazard; container spread needs control
problems.guidance: Extension sources emphasize careful handling of pads and fruit. No species-specific pest or disease profile is established here, and the record does not claim all Opuntia fruit is edible or palatable.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No source evaluates this cactus in hydroponics.

evidence.note: Kew characterizes the species as a succulent shrub or tree.

height.reason: No cultivar- and climate-specific mature dimension is assigned.

spread.reason: No supported spread range is available for the represented plant.

spacing.reason: No exact garden spacing is provided; pad-planting instructions are not spacing guidance.

light.reason: Outdoor arid-culture context is not converted to indoor light intensity.
